archetype.name: Bubble Team (depth-driven)
archetype.definition: A Pittsburgh side whose 5-on-5 shares and penalty kill grade out as a fringe playoff team, held below .500 by bad luck in close games and by a top line that is losing its minutes.

report.headline: Unlucky in close games, but the top line's 5-on-5 slide is real
report.take:
Pittsburgh sits 5-6-1, sixth in the Metropolitan, but the goals say something closer to coin-flip: 40 scored, 40 allowed, a differential of 0. Pts vs Goal Diff has them at -2.4, 30th in the league, so close games have gone the wrong way. Two of their three wins went to overtime. Three losses came by a single goal, one of them in overtime. The underlying play is a little better than average: xGF % of 52.9% and CF % of 52% both rank 12th, and the penalty kill (83.9%, 8th) is well above the league's 78.3%. On that evidence this is a team whose record should drift upward.

The even differential flatters them, though. It includes a 7-0 opening-night win in September. Across the last ten games they are 3-6-1 and -8, scoring 2.7 a game against 3.5 allowed. October as a whole was 4-7 in regulation-decided terms of the monthly line, with 3.64 goals allowed a game. A team being outscored by that much over ten games is not purely unlucky, even with the overtime losses. The losing also came on a heavy road swing through Chicago, Colorado, Vegas and Utah, and they won the next two at home.

The most telling split is who is winning the ice. The top-minute players are underwater at 5-on-5: Sidney Crosby at 44.5% xGF and -6, Rickard Rakell at 44.8%, and Erik Karlsson at 44.3% despite his 12 points. The positive share is coming from the bottom of the lineup: Connor Dewar at 61.1%, Ville Koivunen at 64%, and Nick Robertson at 60% with 6 goals and a +8 that ranks him 11th among left wings. Evgeni Malkin, with 6 goals, 9 points and a 9.4 Game Score, is the one top-six forward driving results. That is why the forward group grades only D+ while the team's possession numbers look fine: the minutes go to the players losing them.

The goaltending is better than its .888 save percentage suggests. Team GSAx of 3.1 is well above the league's 0.822, so the shots Pittsburgh allows are dangerous ones and its goalies are stopping more than expected. Arturs Silovs (1.7 GSAx, 2 shutouts, 12th on the goalie tab) has been the steadier option over Sergei Murashov (-1.4). The defense that does leak is against wingers, who are beating their expected output by 0.65 points a game, 29th in the league. Last season's 98 points came with a 101.2 PDO and the third-best offense. This year's 99.3 PDO points the other way, which leaves room for a bounce.

strengths.title: Winning the 5-on-5 chance battle
strengths.body: Pittsburgh owns 52.9% of the expected goals and 52% of the shot attempts at 5-on-5, both 12th, ahead of a league that averages 50% by definition. Its history backs it: the team has posted a 51-53% xGF in each of the last five seasons apart from 2024-25. A possession edge this steady usually outlasts a cold start.

strengths.title: Penalty kill well above league
strengths.body: An 83.9% kill ranks 8th and sits more than five points above the league average. It is in line with the 84.4% of 2021-22 and better than any season since. It has kept a team that loses at even strength in games it would otherwise have lost by more.

strengths.title: Depth forwards tilting the ice
strengths.body: Robertson, Koivunen and Dewar all sit at 60% xGF or better in bottom-six minutes, and Robertson's 6 goals match Malkin for the team lead. Robertson's shooting will cool, but the chance shares from that group are what keep the team's overall numbers above water.

concerns.title: Top line losing its minutes
concerns.body: Crosby and Rakell each play over 19 minutes a night and are both under 45% xGF. Karlsson, at 23.47 minutes, is at 44.3%. Crosby ranks 154th of 230 centers on the site's tab. Until the first unit breaks even, the team's best players are giving back what the depth earns, which is why the forward grade is a D+.

concerns.title: Differential propped up by opener
concerns.body: The season's even goal differential rests on a 7-0 September win. The last ten games are -8, at 3.5 goals allowed a game. That is too wide a margin to blame only on close-game luck. The recent stretch is a better read of the defense than the season line is.

concerns.title: Wingers feasting against them
concerns.body: Opposing wingers are beating their expected points by 0.65 a game, 29th in the league. Pittsburgh also allows slightly more shots than the league average. The positive team GSAx says the goalies are cleaning up dangerous looks, so the problem is the shots being allowed, not the saves.

trend.note: A 7-0 opener gave way to a four-game losing streak on a western road trip and a 3-6-1 ten-game run. Two straight home wins, a 4-0 shutout of Florida and an overtime win over Nashville, closed the stretch.

weekAhead.headline: Three teams ranked above them, two with leaky penalty kills
weekAhead.body:
All three opponents sit above Pittsburgh's 19th on the site. Pittsburgh lost to two of them in the last ten days: 5-4 at Utah and 6-2 at Vegas. Both rematches are at home. Utah is the heavyweight, 5th on the site with a 58.4% xGF and an A+ blueline. Vegas brings an A-grade forward group and a 0.69 goal differential a game. Montréal is the softest matchup on paper but owns the second-best Pts vs Goal Diff in the league on a zero differential, a mirror image of Pittsburgh's luck.

The opening is special teams and goaltending. Utah's penalty kill is 29th at 66.7% and Vegas's is 28th at 67.7%. Utah's goalies are 31st in GSAx and Vegas's are 23rd. Pittsburgh's 20.6% power play is only middling, but against those kills it should produce. A split of the three games is a fair result, and anything better would be a sign the slide is over.

keyMatchups.title: PK against Utah's league-best power play
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 38.1% of its power plays, first in the league. Pittsburgh's 83.9% kill is its best unit. The 5-4 loss in Utah shows how quickly this game can get away, so staying out of the box matters as much as the kill.

keyMatchups.title: Power play versus leaky kills
keyMatchups.body: Utah and Vegas both kill under 68%, and both get below-average goaltending. Karlsson's 5 power-play points and Novak's 4 lead a unit that should find more chances than usual. Two of these three games are where Pittsburgh's middling power play can swing results.

keyMatchups.title: Defensemen and wingers in Montréal
keyMatchups.body: Montréal's defense gives up more than expected to defensemen (+0.31, 26th) and to wingers (+0.44, 26th). That sets up Karlsson, Letang and the Rakell-Robertson-Koivunen wingers. Montréal's power play is only 12.5%, so even strength decides this one.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Crosby's line can break even at 5-on-5 against Utah. Utah's defense holds centers well under their expected points (6th), and Pittsburgh's top unit is already losing its minutes.

restOfSeason.body:
The case for improvement is solid but not overwhelming. A 30th-ranked Pts vs Goal Diff almost always drifts back toward zero, the 5-on-5 shares rank in the top half, and the goaltending is beating expectations. The current 75-point pace should therefore undersell the finish. The case against is the top of the lineup: the forward group grades D+, and the team was outscored clearly over the last ten games. Neither of those is a luck problem.

What probably regresses: Robertson's scoring rate in fourth-line minutes, and the run of overtime and one-goal losses. What should hold: the penalty kill and the chance share. If the Crosby and Rakell minutes even out, this is the roughly 85-90-point team its process suggests. If they don't, it settles in the low 80s, like 2024-25, chasing a wild card.

confidence.note: Twelve games, and the differential is skewed by one 7-0 win.
